title: Pennoyer v. Neff (1877)
summary: An Oregon default judgment could not support the sale of Neff’s land because the court had not acquired jurisdiction over him or attached the property at the outset.
notes:
Read this as the historical framework developed and qualified by International Shoe, Shaffer, and Burnham. It does not supply the complete modern test. “In personam” concerns personal liability; “in rem” and “quasi in rem” describe forms of adjudication involving property.

Mitchell was an Oregon attorney suing for roughly $300 in unpaid legal fees; he bought Neff's land himself at the sheriff's sale and then conveyed it to Pennoyer, and Justice Field wrote the majority opinion.

Pennoyer's famous rule: every state possesses exclusive jurisdiction over persons and property within its territory and none may exercise direct jurisdiction over persons or property outside it, so a personal judgment against a nonresident who was neither served in the state nor appeared is void.

sections.Parties: Neff claimed land under a federal patent. Pennoyer claimed the same land through an execution sale based on Mitchell’s earlier judgment against Neff for legal services.
sections.Material Facts: Mitchell sued Neff in Oregon while Neff was outside the state. Neff was not personally served in Oregon and did not appear. Mitchell used publication to obtain a default money judgment. The land was later subjected to execution and sold; it had not been attached as the basis for jurisdiction when Mitchell began the original action. Neff relied on his federal patent in disputing the purchaser’s title. The decisive question was the validity of the earlier proceeding, not whether Mitchell had supplied legal services.
sections.Procedural History: Neff sued Pennoyer in federal court to recover the land. The court ruled for Neff because the underlying judgment was invalid. On review, the Supreme Court affirmed. It examined the Oregon judgment collaterally, in the later title litigation, rather than on a direct appeal by Neff from Mitchell’s suit.
sections.Issue: Could publication against an absent nonresident support a personal judgment and a later execution sale when the property had not first been brought under the court’s authority?
sections.Holding: No. The court lacked authority to impose the personal obligation. The subsequent levy did not cure that defect, so the execution purchaser could not rely on the judgment to defeat Neff’s title.
sections.Reasoning: The opinion reasoned from territorial sovereignty. A state could exercise authority over persons within its territory and adjudicate interests in property located there, but its process did not itself compel an absent nonresident to answer personally. A property-based proceeding required the property to be brought under the court’s control at the beginning, with the resulting authority confined to that property. Otherwise a later discovery or seizure of assets could improperly turn an invalid personal judgment into a valid one. Publication might serve a different role in a properly initiated property proceeding; it was inadequate to establish the personal jurisdiction asserted here. The opinion also discusses recognized qualifications involving status, appearance, and consent.

learning.why: An Oregon default judgment could not support the sale of Neff’s land because the court had not acquired jurisdiction over him or attached the property at the outset.

topics.cp-territorial: The historical territorial model distinguishes judgments imposing personal liability from proceedings directed at property.
topics.cp-property-jurisdiction: Attaching property after judgment could not retroactively validate the earlier personal judgment.
topics.cp-collateral: Neff attacked the earlier judgment when litigating title against the purchaser.
topics.cp-notice: Publication alone did not authorize the personal judgment against an absent nonresident.
topics.cp-due-process: Pennoyer is the origin of treating personal jurisdiction as a Fourteenth Amendment due-process limit on state courts.
topics.cp-service: The case holds that substituted service by publication cannot support a personal judgment against a nonresident.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Hunt dissented; the assigned materials principally develop the majority’s territorial account.

mnemonic.rationale: Land sold on a judgment served by newspaper
